# Overview of Models and Functions $\bigstar$

$$\begin{array}{llll}
\hline
\text{Week 3 model}
&
\text{its }\theta\text{ lives in}
&
\theta_i=h(X_i'\beta)
&
\text{the regression}
\\
\hline
\text{Normal, mean }\mu
&
(-\infty,\infty)
&
\mu_i=X_i'\beta
&
\text{OLS (the hook)}
\\
\text{Bernoulli, prob. }p
&
(0,1)
&
p_i=\Lambda(X_i'\beta)
=\dfrac{e^{X_i'\beta}}{1+e^{X_i'\beta}}
&
\text{logit}
\\
\text{Bernoulli, prob. }p
&
(0,1)
&
p_i=\Phi(X_i'\beta)
&
\text{probit}
\\
\text{Poisson, rate }\theta
&
(0,\infty)
&
\theta_i=e^{X_i'\beta}
&
\text{Poisson regression}
\\
\hline
\end{array}$$

- $\Lambda$ and $\Phi$ are S-curves from $0$ to $1$ (the logistic and normal CDFs); $e^{(\cdot)}$ is positive.

- The **link function** is the inverse, $g=h^{-1}$, mapping $\theta$ back to the line:

$g(p)=\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right), \qquad g(\theta)=\log\theta.$

Textbooks start from $g$; think in $h$.

- Every row is a *generalized linear model*.

## Connect to Log Likelihood $\bigstar$

Substitute $\theta_i=h(X_i'\beta)$ into Week 3's log-likelihood:

$$\ell(\beta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\log f(y_i\mid\theta_i),
\qquad
\theta_i=h(X_i'\beta).$$

- **Estimate:** the peak, in $k$ dimensions. [No closed form except OLS]{.underline}; Newton-Raphson, which `glm()` runs in a few steps.

- **Standard errors:** the **square root of the inverse of the negative curvature** of the log-likelihood at the peak. `summary()` prints the square roots.

::: callout-tip
$$\widehat{SE}(\hat\theta)=\sqrt{\left[-\ell''(\hat\theta)\right]^{-1}}$$

The variance of MLE is one over minus the second derivative of the log-likelihood at its peak.

$$\widehat{V}(\hat{\theta}) = \left[ -\left. \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta^2} \right|_{\hat{\theta}} \right]^{-1} = \frac{1}{\text{observed information}}$$
:::

- **Tests:** `summary()`'s $z$ is Wald; `anova()` is LR.

- **Comparison:** AIC and BIC from $\ell(\hat{\beta})$.

- **Interpretation:** $\beta_j$ moves the line; how much it moves $\theta_i$ depends on $h$ and on where person $i$ sits.

::: callout-note
$$\eta_i=X_i'\beta, \qquad \theta_i=h(\eta_i)=h(X_i'\beta)$$ For the linear predictor, the effect of $X_i'$ on $\eta_i$ is $\beta$.

Using the chain rule,

$$\frac{\partial \theta_i}{\partial x_{ij}}
=
h'(\eta_i)\beta_j$$ Now $h'(\eta_i)\beta_j$ depends on $h$ and on where observation $i$ is on that curve.

For OLS, $h(\eta)=\eta$, $h'(\eta)=1$, thus the effect of $X_i'$ is constant.

For logit, $p_i=\Lambda(\eta_i)$

$$\Lambda'(\eta_i)=p_i(1-p_i) $$

$$\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial x_{ij}} = \beta_jp_i(1-p_i)$$

Two people can therefore have the same $\beta_j$ but different probability changes because they have different $X_i$ and hence different baseline probabilities $p_i$.

For Poisson, $\theta_i=e^{\eta_i}$

$$\frac{\partial \theta_i}{\partial x_{ij}}
=
\beta_j e^{\eta_i}
=
\beta_j\theta_i$$

The effect depends on where person $i$ sits.
:::

# Binary

Two ways for the same model:

$$\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = X_i'\beta $$ Or

$$p_i=\Lambda(X_i'\beta)
=\dfrac{e^{X_i'\beta}}{1+e^{X_i'\beta}}$$

- $\Lambda$ is the inverse of the log-odds

- $1-p_i = \frac{1}{1+e^{X_i'\beta}}$

## Logit: The S-Curve $\bigstar$

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Base R: logistic inverse-link h(X'beta)

eta <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 1000)

# logistic function
h <- function(eta) {
  1 / (1 + exp(-eta))
}

p <- h(eta)

# plotting region
par(mar = c(4, 5, 2, 3))

plot(
  eta, p,
  type = "l",
  lwd = 3,
  col = "navy",
  xlim = c(-6.5, 6.7),
  ylim = c(0, 1.12),
  axes = FALSE,
  xlab = "",
  ylab = ""
)

# axes with arrows
arrows(-6.3, 0, 6.6, 0,
       length = 0.08)

arrows(0, 0, 0, 1.10,
       length = 0.08)

# x-axis labels
axis(
  1,
  at = c(-6, -4, -2, 2, 4, 6),
  labels = c("-6", "-4", "-2", "2", "4", "6"),
  tick = FALSE
)

# reference lines
segments(-6.3, 0.5, 0, 0.5,
         lty = 2,
         col = "grey50")

segments(-6.3, 1, 6, 1,
         lty = 2,
         col = "grey50")

# labels
text(-6.4, 0.5, "0.5",
     pos = 2,
     col = "grey50")

text(6.5, 1, "1",
     pos = 4,
     col = "grey50")

text(0, 1.1,
     expression(theta),
     pos = 3,
     cex = 1.2)

text(6.65, 0,
     expression(X^prime * beta),
     pos = 4,
     cex = 1.2)

# point at eta = 0
points(0, 0.5,
       pch = 19,
       col = "orangered3")

# tangent at eta = 0
# logistic derivative at 0 = 0.25
x_tan <- seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 100)
y_tan <- 0.5 + 0.25 * x_tan

lines(
  x_tan, y_tan,
  col = "orangered3",
  lwd = 2
)

# annotation
text(
  1.5, 0.30,
  "slope 0.25 at 0",
  col = "orangered3",
  pos = 4,
  cex = 1.05
)
```

- $\Lambda$ is an S-surve, flat near 0 and 1, steepest at $\theta = 0.5$ ($X'\beta = 0$). Any real $X'\beta$ ($p$) lands inside (0, 1)

- The slope of $X'\beta$ is $\theta(1-\theta)$: one unit moves the probability by up to 0.25 in the middle and almost nothing in the tails.

::: callout-note
$$\theta=\Lambda(\eta)=\frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta},
\qquad \eta=X'\beta$$

$$\frac{d\theta}{d\eta}
=
\frac{e^\eta(1+e^\eta)-e^\eta e^\eta}{(1+e^\eta)^2}
=
\frac{e^\eta}{(1+e^\eta)^2}$$

$$\theta(1-\theta)
=
\frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta}
\frac{1}{1+e^\eta}
=
\frac{e^\eta}{(1+e^\eta)^2}$$

$$\boxed{\frac{d\theta}{d(X'\beta)}=\theta(1-\theta)}$$
:::

- Only 0s and 1s are observed on the vertical axis

### Connect Logit to Log Likelihood $\bigstar$

$$\ell(\beta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
y_i\log p_i
+
(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)
\right]
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
y_iX_i'\beta
-
\log\left(1+e^{X_i'\beta}\right)
\right]$$

Or

$$\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
=
X_i'\beta,
\qquad
\log(1-p_i)
=
-\log\left(1+e^{X_i'\beta}\right).$$

### Newton's Method

$$\beta^{[t+1]}
=
\beta^{[t]}
+
\mathcal{I}\left(\beta^{[t]}\right)^{-1}
S\left(\beta^{[t]}\right),
\qquad
S(\beta)
=
\sum_i (y_i-p_i)X_i,
\qquad
\mathcal{I}(\beta)
=
\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)X_iX_i'$$

### Interpret the Coefficient $\bigstar$

If $\hat{\beta} = 0.391$

$$\begin{array}{llll}
\hline
\text{Scale}
&
\text{Quantity}
&
\hat{\beta}=0.391\text{ says}
&
\\
\hline
\text{Log-odds}
&
\log\left(\dfrac{p}{1-p}\right)=X'\beta
&
\text{one more word adds }0.391
&
\text{linear, not intuitive}
\\
\text{Odds}
&
\dfrac{p}{1-p}=e^{X'\beta}
&
\text{odds multiply by }e^{0.391}=1.48
&
\text{the odds ratio}
\\
\text{Probability}
&
p=\Lambda(X'\beta)
&
\text{depends on where you start}
&
\text{what we care about}
\\
\hline
\end{array}$$

::: callout-warning
An odds ratio is not a risk ratio and **not a difference in probabilities**.

Report on the probability scale, and say *for whom*.
:::

::: callout-tip
### Conversion Across Scales

1.  Start from the linear predictor $X'\beta$
2.  Convert log-odds to odds $odds = p/(1-p)= exp(X'\beta)$
3.  Convert odds to probability $p = exp(X'\beta)/(exp(X'\beta)+1)$
:::

### Average Marginal Effect $\bigstar$

For one person, the slope of the probability with respect to $X_j$ is $\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial X_{ij}} = p_i(1-p_i)\beta_j$, so $\beta_j$ is scaled by where the person sits on the S-curve

- **Average Marginal Effect (AME)**: compute the marginal effect separately for every actual observation, then average those marginal effects.

- **Marginal Effect at the Mean (MEM):** create one hypothetical observation with every covariate set to its sample mean, compute its predicted probability, and then compute the marginal effect at that point.

`avg_slopes()` reports both MEM and AME

[**AME** (observed-value approach; Hanmer and Kalkan 2013) is recommended,]{.underline} because:

- An “average” case may not correspond to any real person, so MEM can evaluate the model at an unrealistic combination of covariates.

- For non-linear models, the effect of $\beta_j$ on $p_i$ on where person $i$ sits. (see the call-out under \[**Connect to Log Likelihood**\].)

#### Calculate SE of the AME

- Delta Method

- Simulation

- Bootstrap

**Never build an interval on the log-odds scale and transform its endpoints if what you want is an interval for a difference in probabilities.**

::: callout-note
An example:

In a logit regression

$$\text{logit}(p)=\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\eta$$

Its inversion $$p = \eta^-1 = \frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta}$$

If we want to compare two log-odds $\eta_1=\beta_0+\beta_1,\qquad \eta_0=\beta_0$

The difference of probability is

$$\Delta p=p_1-p_0=\frac{e^{\eta_1}}{1+e^{\eta_1}}-\frac{e^{\eta_0}}{1+e^{\eta_0}}$$

And

$$\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_1-\eta_0)=\frac{e^{\eta_1-\eta_0}}{1+e^{\eta_1-\eta_0}}$$

$$\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_1)-\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_0)=\frac{e^{\eta_1}}{1+e^{\eta_1}}-\frac{e^{\eta_0}}{1+e^{\eta_0}}$$

Clearly

$$\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_1-\eta_0)\neq\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_1)-\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_0)$$
:::
